newsitem.title: USA: US bonds end lower, fear of Fed rate hike revived.
newsitem.headline: US bonds end lower, fear of Fed rate hike revived.

text.p: U.S. Treasury prices ended lower on Tuesday after investors began to look toward next week's Federal Reserve policy meeting and to focus on the possibility of another interest-rate hike, analysts said.

The bond market got good news near the start of the trading session. The government reported that retail sales fell 0.3 percent in April. Excluding vehicle sales, which the auto industry had reported to be depressed, retail sales were down 0.1 percent.

The 0.3 percent decline had been forecast but the 0.1 percent slippage in sales excluding auto transactions was even weaker than the slight 0.1 percent rise that had been forecast. In addition, March sales data were also revised downward -- to flat for total retail sales and to a slight rise of 0.1 percent with auto sales excluded.
The market rose to session highs on the retail sales data. The 30-year bond rose to 97-4/32; its yield fell to 6.85 pct.
But those levels could not hold, analysts said, not with a Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) monetary policy meeting just a week away and its outcome still uncertain.
As a consequence, the 30-year bond finished nearly a point below its session highs - at 96-8/32, its yield at 6.92 pct.
The two-year note, yielding 6.20 percent one half hour after the retail sales data were released, ended at 100-6/32 on Tuesday, down 3/32, its yield having risen to 6.27 percent.

"The two-year note aat 6.20 percent, just 70 basis points from the (5.50 percent) federal funds rate, was just not correctly priced," said Chris Rupkey, vice president and financial economist at Bank of Tokyo/Mitsubishi. "We hit the barrier. We couldn't go any further without seeing what the Fed is going to do (at its May 20 FOMC policy meeting)."

Prices weakened at mid-morning after the Atlanta Federal Reserve Bank reported that its business activity index jumped to 22.1 in April from a revised 8.6 percent in March. In the Chicago futures market, the June T-bond contract slipped to 109-16/32, below the 200-day moving average of 110-3/32.

A contrary view to the Atlanta Fed's index was presented by the Richmond Fed, which reported that its Manufacturing shipments index fell to 15 in April, from 29 previously, and that its service revenues index fell to 33 from 43 in March.

"We usually don't give more weight to the Atlanta Fed index than to the monthly retail sales data and yet that is what happened," said Patrick Dimick, trader and Treasury market strategist at UBS Securities Inc. "So many of the shorts have covered that there is no longer the underlying bias to grind higher that we have experienced ever since the first-quarter Employment Cost Index and the March durable goods orders came in weaker than expected," he said. "From trading near new highs, the market collapsed."
Abetting that collapse was a Reuters interview with sources close to the Fed, market participants said.

While investors have been gradually stepping back from the notion that another Fed interest-rate hike will occur next week, the Reuters story said the Fed is likely to raise the federal funds rate by 25 basis points next week to stop the economy from potentially overheating.

"The story definitely tagged a quarter point onto the afternoon's losses," said Dimick. "The market was clearly leaning to the downside, but the story really pushed us in that direction. It had a pretty sizable impact."

On Tuesday, three-month bill rates slipped two basis points to 5.07 percent and six-month bill rates rose one basis point to 5.33 percent. Year bill rates rose four basis points to 5.55 percent. Five-year notes closed at 100-8/32, down 8/32, to yield 6.56 percent. Ten-year notes fell 21/32 to 96-27/32 to yield 6.71 percent.
